title: Embeddings & semantic similarity
summary: Turn text into vectors so a computer can measure meaning, then use distance to find what is semantically similar.
objectives: Explain what a text embedding is and why it is a vector
Describe how similar meanings map to nearby vectors
Compute cosine similarity between two embeddings
Generate embeddings with a real embeddings API
Build a tiny semantic search over a list of documents
Know when to use embeddings versus keyword search
Recognise embeddings as the foundation of RAG

options: A compressed copy of the text
A list of numbers (a vector) representing the meaning of the text
A summary written by the model
The raw token IDs of the text
quiz.why: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers; texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions.

quiz.q: Two sentences with similar meaning will have embeddings that are...
options: Far apart / pointing in different directions
Close together / pointing in a similar direction
quiz.why: Semantic similarity shows up as geometric closeness: similar meaning means a small angle between the vectors.

quiz.q: Which measure is most commonly used to compare two embeddings?
quiz.why: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude, so it captures direction (meaning).

quiz.q: Cosine similarity returns 1.0 for two vectors. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: They point in exactly the same direction, so the texts are maximally similar in meaning.
quiz.why: Cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1; 1 means identical direction, 0 means unrelated, and negative means opposite direction.

quiz.q: Why would you choose embeddings over plain keyword search?
quiz.answer: Embeddings match on meaning, so they find relevant results even when the exact words differ (e.g. 'car' vs 'automobile').
quiz.why: Keyword search needs matching words; embeddings capture semantic meaning, handling synonyms and paraphrases.

quiz.q: Embeddings are the first step in which common LLM pattern?
quiz.why: RAG embeds your documents, retrieves the most similar ones to a question, and feeds them to the model as context.

body_markdown:
## What is an embedding?

An **embedding** is a list of numbers — a **vector** — that represents the *meaning* of a piece of text. A model reads your sentence and outputs something like `[0.12, -0.04, 0.88, ...]`, often with hundreds or a thousand dimensions.

As a maths graduate you already have the intuition: a vector is just a point in space. The whole trick of embeddings is that **texts with similar meaning land near each other** in that space, and unrelated texts land far apart.

## Meaning becomes geometry

Once text is a vector, *similarity becomes distance*. "How is the weather?" and "What's it like outside?" use almost no shared words, but their embeddings point in nearly the same direction.

This is powerful because it turns a fuzzy language question ("do these mean the same thing?") into a concrete maths question ("how close are these two vectors?").

## Cosine similarity

The most common way to compare two embeddings is **cosine similarity** — the cosine of the angle between them. It ignores how long the vectors are and only cares about *direction*.

- `1.0` -> same direction (very similar meaning)
- `0.0` -> perpendicular (unrelated)
- `-1.0` -> opposite direction

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

print(cosine_similarity([1, 0, 1], [1, 0, 1]))   # 1.0
print(cosine_similarity([1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]))   # 0.0
```

## Generating real embeddings

You rarely build embeddings by hand — you call an embeddings API. Install a provider's client, set your API key as an environment variable, and ask for a vector per text.

```bash
pip install voyageai
export VOYAGE_API_KEY="your-key-here"
```

```python
import voyageai

vo = voyageai.Client()   # reads VOYAGE_API_KEY from the environment

docs = ["How do I reset my password?", "What is your refund policy?"]
result = vo.embed(docs, model="voyage-3", input_type="document")
vectors = result.embeddings   # one vector per document
print(len(vectors), len(vectors[0]))   # 2 vectors, each ~1024 numbers
```

## A tiny semantic search

Put it together: embed your documents once, embed the user's question, then rank documents by cosine similarity. The top match is your most relevant document — even if it shares no words with the question.

```python
query = "I forgot my login details"
q_vec = vo.embed([query], model="voyage-3", input_type="query").embeddings[0]

scores = [cosine_similarity(q_vec, d) for d in vectors]
best = docs[scores.index(max(scores))]
print(best)   # 'How do I reset my password?'
```

## Why this matters

Embeddings are the foundation of **RAG** (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): embed your knowledge base, retrieve the chunks most similar to a question, then hand those chunks to Claude as context. Master embeddings now and the next lessons on vector databases and RAG will click into place.

## Your task

Embed five short sentences of your own, compute the cosine similarity of every pair, and confirm that the pairs *you* think are similar score highest.

slides.title: Embeddings & semantic similarity
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Three, where we build real A I application skills. In this lesson we tackle embeddings and semantic similarity. By the end you'll understand how to turn text into numbers a computer can compare, how to measure whether two pieces of text mean the same thing, and why this single idea powers modern search and retrieval. As a maths graduate, you're going to feel right at home here.

slides.title: What is an embedding?
bullets: An embedding is a vector of numbers.
It represents the meaning of some text.
Often hundreds or a thousand dimensions.
Similar meanings sit close together.
slides.narration: Let's start with the core idea. An embedding is simply a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a piece of text. You feed in a sentence, and the model gives you back something like a thousand numbers. You already know vectors as points in space. The magic is that texts with similar meaning end up as points that are close together.

slides.title: Meaning becomes geometry
bullets: Similarity turns into distance.
Close vectors mean similar meaning.
Different words can still be close.
A fuzzy question becomes a maths one.
slides.narration: Here's why this is so useful. Once a sentence is a vector, the question do these two sentences mean the same thing becomes how close are these two vectors. How is the weather and what's it like outside share almost no words, yet their vectors point in nearly the same direction. We've turned a fuzzy language problem into a clean geometry problem.

slides.title: Cosine similarity
bullets: Measures the angle between vectors.
1.0 means same direction, very similar.
0.0 means unrelated.
Ignores length, only cares about direction.
slides.narration: So how do we measure closeness? The standard tool is cosine similarity, which is just the cosine of the angle between two vectors. A value of one means they point the same way, so the meanings are very similar. Zero means they're unrelated. It ignores how long the vectors are and focuses purely on direction, which is exactly what we want when comparing meaning.

slides.title: Cosine similarity in code
bullets: A few lines with NumPy.
Dot product over the product of norms.
Easy to test on toy vectors first.
slides.narration: Cosine similarity is only a few lines of code. We take the dot product of the two vectors and divide by the product of their lengths, their norms. Notice this is exactly the formula from your linear algebra classes. Try it first on tiny toy vectors so you can see one point zero for identical vectors and zero for perpendicular ones, before you ever touch real data.

slides.title: Generating real embeddings
bullets: You call an embeddings API, not build it.
Keep your key in an environment variable.
One vector comes back per text.
slides.code:
import voyageai
vo = voyageai.Client()  # reads VOYAGE_API_KEY

docs = ["reset my password", "refund policy"]
res = vo.embed(docs, model="voyage-3",
               input_type="document")
vectors = res.embeddings
slides.narration: In practice you never compute embeddings by hand. You call an embeddings A P I. Install the provider's client, store your A P I key in an environment variable so it never ends up in your code, and pass in a list of texts. You get back one vector per text. Here we embed two short documents and collect their vectors, ready to compare.

slides.title: A tiny semantic search
bullets: Embed your documents once.
Embed the user's question.
Rank documents by cosine similarity.
Top score is the best match.
slides.code:
q = vo.embed(["I forgot my login"],
             model="voyage-3",
             input_type="query").embeddings[0]
scores = [cos(q, d) for d in vectors]
best = docs[scores.index(max(scores))]
slides.narration: Now we put it together into a tiny semantic search. Embed all your documents once and store the vectors. When a question comes in, embed that too, then score every document by its cosine similarity to the question. The highest score is your best match. The beautiful part is that I forgot my login matches reset my password, even though they share no words at all.

slides.title: Embeddings vs keyword search
bullets: Keyword search needs matching words.
Embeddings match on meaning.
Handles synonyms and paraphrases.
Use keywords for exact codes and IDs.
slides.narration: When should you reach for embeddings instead of plain keyword search? Keyword search only finds documents that contain the exact words you typed. Embeddings match on meaning, so they handle synonyms and rephrasings, finding car when you searched automobile. That said, for exact matches like product codes, order numbers, or I Ds, a simple keyword lookup is still the right tool.

slides.title: Why this matters: RAG
bullets: Embeddings are the base of RAG.
Embed your knowledge base.
Retrieve the most similar chunks.
Feed them to Claude as context.
slides.narration: Here's where this is all heading. Embeddings are the foundation of retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. The idea is simple: embed your whole knowledge base, retrieve the chunks most similar to a user's question, and hand those chunks to Claude as context so it can answer accurately from your own data. Everything you learn today is the groundwork for the vector database and RAG lessons coming next.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: An embedding is a meaning vector.
Cosine similarity measures closeness.
Embed, then rank by similarity to search.
Embeddings power RAG.
Task: compare five of your own sentences.
slides.narration: Let's recap. An embedding turns text into a vector that captures meaning. Cosine similarity measures how close two vectors point, and therefore how similar two texts are. To search, you embed your documents and rank them by similarity to the question. And this whole pipeline is the foundation of RAG. Your task before next time: embed five short sentences of your own, compute the cosine similarity of every pair, and check that the pairs you'd call similar really do score highest. Great work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
